prompt: Your monorepo's release train merges dozens of branches at 09:00, which triggers around 30 concurrent PR review jobs. Roughly a third fail with 429 rate_limit_error, the check turns red, and developers re-run the job by hand until it passes. The reviewer is advisory and not a merge blocker. What change most reliably eliminates the manual re-runs?

options.text: Move the review to the Message Batches API so the 09:00 burst is absorbed by the batch queue and processed at half the token cost.
options.explanation: Batches can take up to 24 hours to complete, so a PR review that developers expect on the pull request within minutes would arrive after they have moved on. The cost saving is real, but it trades away the timeliness that makes PR feedback useful; the burst problem needs flow control, not asynchronous delivery.

options.text: Wrap the claude -p call in a retry loop of three attempts spaced one second apart so transient limit errors clear before the step fails.
options.explanation: Thirty jobs retrying in lockstep one second apart re-create the same burst three times and typically exhaust the limit again before it resets. Fixed short intervals ignore the retry-after guidance the API returns, so the loop mostly converts one failure into three and still leaves the check red.

options.text: Cap concurrent review jobs with a CI concurrency group and retry with exponential backoff and jitter that honours retry-after.
options.explanation: The failures come from too many simultaneous requests, so limiting how many jobs run at once removes the cause, and backoff with jitter that waits as long as retry-after asks handles the residual collisions without stampeding. Together they let every job eventually complete on its own, which is what removes the manual re-runs.

options.text: Split each review into one request per changed file so every call is small and stays well under the per-request token limits.
options.explanation: The 429 is a rate limit on requests and tokens per minute, not a per-request size problem, so turning 30 reviews into hundreds of small requests multiplies the request count and makes the burst worse. It also strips the cross-file context that a review of a multi-file change depends on.

prompt: A developer disputes a review finding that claims a new handler bypasses the auth middleware. The review ran headlessly on an ephemeral runner that was destroyed after the job, and the only artifact is the final markdown comment. Your team wants to see which files Claude actually read and which Grep calls it made before it wrote that finding. What should the job capture going forward?

options.text: Run with --output-format stream-json --verbose and upload the full event stream as a CI artifact alongside the posted comment.
options.explanation: The stream-json output records every tool call, its input and its result, plus the assistant turns in between, so the team can replay exactly which files were read and which searches ran before the finding. Archiving it as a job artifact survives the runner teardown, which is the thing that made the current dispute unresolvable.

options.text: Add a prompt instruction telling Claude to list every file it inspected and every search it ran inside the review comment itself.
options.explanation: A self-reported list is generated by the model from memory of its own trace and can omit or misstate steps, so it cannot serve as evidence in a dispute. It also bloats every review comment with a provenance dump that developers have to scroll past on the many findings nobody contests.

options.text: Persist the session id and, when a finding is disputed, run claude --resume on a fresh runner to ask what it looked at.
options.explanation: Session state lives on the machine that ran the job, and the ephemeral runner was destroyed, so there is nothing for a new runner to resume. Even when a session can be resumed, asking the model afterwards what it looked at is a recollection, not the recorded tool trace the team needs.

options.text: Re-run the same review job with the same prompt on the disputed PR and compare the two sets of findings to see whether the claim holds up.
options.explanation: A second run explores the repository along a different path and may read different files, so agreement or disagreement between runs says nothing about what the original review inspected. It costs a full review to produce a new opinion when the question was about the evidence behind the old one.

prompt: Your review step has a 10-minute CI timeout. On pull requests touching more than 25 files, Claude Code keeps exploring related modules and the runner kills it at the deadline with no output at all, so the check shows a hard failure and no findings. Average PRs finish in about three minutes. You want large PRs to still return whatever review is possible. What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Raise the CI step timeout to 60 minutes so exploration of large pull requests can run to completion before the runner intervenes.
options.explanation: A longer deadline only moves the cliff: a 40-file PR can still exhaust it, and in the meantime the job ties up a runner and spends tokens on open-ended exploration for most of an hour. It leaves the behaviour unbounded and trades cost and runner capacity for an outcome that is still not guaranteed.

options.text: Split large pull requests into one review job per file with a CI matrix so each job stays comfortably inside the 10-minute limit.
options.explanation: Per-file jobs finish on time but each one reviews a fragment in isolation, so defects that only appear across files, such as a changed signature and its callers in another module, are invisible to every job. The timeout is fixed at the price of the cross-file reasoning that large PRs need most.

options.text: Switch to --output-format stream-json and post whatever findings have been emitted at the moment the runner kills the process.
options.explanation: Findings are normally produced at the end after exploration, so at the moment of the kill the stream usually contains tool calls and reasoning but few or no conclusions. Harvesting a truncated stream also posts partial, unreviewed output whose scope the developer cannot tell from a complete review.

options.text: Bound the run with --max-turns and a prompt that scopes exploration to the diff, then emit a clearly labelled partial review.
options.explanation: The failure is unbounded exploration, so capping agentic turns with --max-turns and telling Claude to prioritise the changed files guarantees the run ends inside the deadline with findings in hand. Labelling the result as partial when the cap was hit keeps the developer informed rather than presenting a truncated review as complete.

prompt: Your chat widget shows nothing while the agent works. For a typical refund the agent calls get_customer, then lookup_order, then process_refund before its reply appears, and customers see a blank screen for 8 to 12 seconds. Abandonment during that gap is measurable. Resolution accuracy is fine and backend latency is already optimised. What should you change?

options.text: Prefetch get_customer and lookup_order from the widget before the first model call so the agent starts with the data in context.
options.explanation: Speculative lookups before the model has read the message fetch data for every conversation, including the many where the customer only asks a policy question, and they need an order id the customer has not supplied yet. It shaves one or two round-trips in some cases but still leaves the screen blank while the rest run.

options.text: Stream the response and turn tool-use events into status lines such as "Checking your order" while calls run.
options.explanation: The wait is not shorter, but the customer sees progress within the first second and every subsequent step, which is what reduces abandonment during multi-tool turns. Streaming also delivers the final reply token by token instead of after the whole turn completes, so perceived latency falls without touching accuracy or the backend.

options.text: Lower max_tokens on every request so the model produces shorter intermediate reasoning and reaches its tool calls faster.
options.explanation: Most of the 8 to 12 seconds is spent in three sequential tool round-trips, not in generating long text, so a lower output cap barely moves the number. It does risk truncating the final customer-facing explanation on complex refunds, which harms the resolution quality that is currently fine.

options.text: Route every turn to a smaller, faster model so each of the three model calls in the refund path completes in less wall-clock time.
options.explanation: The scenario handles high-ambiguity returns and billing disputes, and trading model capability across all turns to save a fraction of a second per call risks the escalation and policy judgement the 80% resolution target depends on. The blank screen would also remain, just for slightly less time.

prompt: Your system prompt is about 14,000 tokens: refund and returns policy, escalation rules, and the four MCP tool definitions. You enabled prompt caching but the dashboard shows almost no cache reads. Inspecting the prompt, the first line is Current time: 2026-09-03T10:42:17Z, refreshed on every turn, followed by the customer's name and then the policy text. What is the fix?

options.text: Summarise the policy and escalation sections down to roughly 3,000 tokens so the uncached cost per turn becomes acceptable.
options.explanation: Compressing the policy shrinks the bill but does not restore caching, and it throws away the exact refund windows and escalation conditions the agent must apply on ambiguous cases. Accepting a permanent cache miss when the miss has a simple structural cause is the wrong trade.

options.text: Move the cache_control breakpoint to the last user message so the whole conversation prefix is cached on each turn.
options.explanation: Caching matches on an exact prefix from the first token, so a breakpoint further down does nothing while the very first line of the system prompt changes every turn. Every request still starts with a different timestamp, so every lookup misses regardless of where the breakpoint sits.

options.text: Put tools, then policy, then customer details and timestamp, with the breakpoint after the policy block.
options.explanation: Cache hits require the cached prefix to be byte-identical, so the static 14,000 tokens must come first and the per-turn timestamp and per-customer details must follow the breakpoint. This keeps the expensive part cached across every turn and every customer while still giving the model the current time and name.

options.text: Remove the timestamp from the prompt and expose a get_current_time MCP tool the agent calls when it needs the date.
options.explanation: This removes the churn but adds a tool round-trip to every conversation that reasons about return windows, which is most of them, and the customer's name still sits ahead of the policy text and breaks the shared prefix across customers. Reordering achieves the cache hit without adding latency.

prompt: About 30% of chats are from customers who contacted support in the previous week. Each new chat starts a fresh Agent SDK session, so the agent asks them to re-explain the issue, re-verifies identity, and sometimes contradicts a commitment made yesterday such as a promised return label. Satisfaction on repeat contacts is 20 points lower. How should the agent carry knowledge across sessions?

options.text: Store the previous session id per customer and resume it with the SDK when they return so the full conversation is already in context.
options.explanation: Resumed sessions carry every earlier tool result and detour, so a customer on their third contact starts with a large, mostly irrelevant context that may already have been compacted into lossy summaries. It also ties the new conversation to whatever state the old one ended in, including a half-finished tool sequence.

options.text: Write a structured case record per session (open issues, commitments, order ids) and inject it into the next session.
options.explanation: A compact, structured record captures exactly what the next session needs, the open issue, what was promised and which orders are involved, without the noise of the full transcript. It is cheap to inject on every turn, avoids the contradictions about commitments, and keeps each customer's history isolated to that customer.

options.text: Prepend the full transcripts of the customer's previous conversations to the first user message so nothing said before is lost.
options.explanation: Raw transcripts grow with every contact and are dominated by greetings, verification steps and tool payloads, so the commitment about a return label is buried in thousands of tokens and easy to miss. It also inflates cost on every turn of the new session for information a short record conveys better.

options.text: Let the agent append free-form notes to a shared memory file that all support sessions load, so learned context accumulates over time.
options.explanation: A memory shared by every session mixes one customer's order numbers and refund history into the context of every other customer's conversation, which is a privacy problem as well as a source of confusion. Free-form notes also have no structure the agent can reliably retrieve a specific commitment from.

prompt: Engineers use the agent to fix failing tests in a legacy service. Each Bash run of the suite prints about 40,000 lines of framework logging and stack traces into the conversation. After two or three runs the agent starts losing track of which fix it already tried and the session degrades. The engineers need the exact failing assertion text to make fixes. What should you change?

options.text: Enable the 1M-token context window for these sessions so several full test runs fit in context without triggering compaction.
options.explanation: A larger window postpones the problem rather than solving it: three or four runs of 40,000 lines still consume most of it, cost rises steeply per turn, and the model still has to pick assertion text out of a haystack of framework logging. The noise is the issue, not the ceiling.

options.text: Add a prompt instruction telling the agent to ignore framework logging in test output and focus only on the assertion messages.
options.explanation: By the time the instruction applies, the 40,000 lines are already in the context and counted against it, so ignoring them saves attention but not tokens. Compaction still fires after a few runs and the agent still forgets what it tried, because the raw output was never kept out of the conversation.

options.text: Delegate each test run to a subagent whose context absorbs the output, and have it return a short summary to the main conversation.
options.explanation: A subagent keeps the logs out of the main context, but the engineers need exact assertion text and file locations, which a summarising step can paraphrase or drop. It also adds a full model round-trip per run to do what a shell filter does deterministically in milliseconds.

options.text: Have the suite run with a quiet reporter, redirect the full log to a file, and let the agent Grep that file for failures.
options.explanation: Redirecting output to a file keeps the 40,000 lines out of the context entirely, and a targeted Grep for failure markers pulls back only the exact assertion lines and paths the engineers need, verbatim. Encoding this in CLAUDE.md makes every session do it by default without summarisation or extra model calls.

prompt: Your codebase-exploration workflow fans out to several .claude/agents subagents that run Grep, Glob and Read to locate call sites, then the main agent explains a legacy module to the engineer. Per-question cost has tripled since the fan-out was added; traces show 80% of tokens are spent in the exploration subagents on mechanical searching, while the explanation quality comes from the final synthesis. How do you reduce cost?

options.text: Set model: haiku in the exploration subagents' frontmatter and leave the main agent on the stronger model for synthesis.
options.explanation: The subagents do mechanical search-and-report work where a smaller model is adequate, and they account for most of the spend, so pointing them at a faster, cheaper model removes the bulk of the cost. Keeping the main agent on the stronger model preserves the synthesis quality the engineers actually value.

options.text: Switch the whole session to a smaller model so both the exploration and the final explanation run at the lower per-token price.
options.explanation: Explaining a legacy module well is the hard reasoning step, and it is the part engineers rate the workflow on. Downgrading it to save the remaining 20% of tokens risks shallow or wrong explanations, when the expensive mechanical searching can be moved to a cheaper model on its own.

options.text: Generate a repository map once and store it in CLAUDE.md so the subagents can answer from it instead of searching each time.
options.explanation: A static map goes stale with every merge and grows into a large block loaded on every turn of every session, which adds cost rather than removing it. It also does not tell the agent where a specific function is called today, which is exactly what the searches exist to find.

options.text: Lower each exploration subagent's turn limit so searches terminate earlier and fewer tokens are spent per question.
options.explanation: Cutting turns makes explorers stop before they have located all call sites, so the synthesis works from incomplete evidence and the explanation quality drops. It reduces tokens per subagent somewhat but leaves every remaining token at the expensive model's price.

prompt: Each extraction request carries a 12,000-token static prefix: the field definitions, twenty worked examples and the JSON schema, with cache_control on the last static block and the document after it. Documents arrive in bursts of 50 to 100 with idle gaps of 20 to 40 minutes between bursts. Billing shows cache reads only for the first few minutes of each burst, then full-price input tokens. What is the right fix?

options.text: Send a lightweight keep-alive request every four minutes during idle gaps so the cached prefix never expires between bursts.
options.explanation: Keeping the cache warm with synthetic requests works only while the scheduler is reliable, adds traffic that counts against rate limits, and pays a cache read plus a small output on every ping around the clock. It is a workaround for a lifetime that can simply be configured longer.

options.text: Place the document before the static prefix so the cached block is the last thing in the prompt and stays hot regardless of gaps.
options.explanation: Caching is prefix-based, so putting the varying document first means the bytes before the breakpoint change on every request and nothing is ever reused. This turns an intermittent miss into a guaranteed miss and moves the schema after the document, which also weakens long-document placement guidance.

options.text: Move the bursts to the Message Batches API, where requests in the same batch share the cached prefix across the whole run.
options.explanation: Batch requests can benefit from caching but hits are not guaranteed because they are processed independently and in no set order, and batches introduce up to 24 hours of latency. It changes the delivery model of the pipeline to address what is a cache lifetime setting.

options.text: Set ttl: "1h" on the static block's cache_control so the cached prefix survives the idle gaps between bursts.
options.explanation: The default cache lifetime is five minutes, refreshed on each hit, so a 20 to 40 minute gap lets it expire and each burst starts by rewriting the prefix. The extended one-hour TTL keeps the 12,000-token prefix alive across the gaps for a higher write price that a burst of 50 reads repays many times over.

prompt: A new customer sends 60-page utility invoices with up to 900 line items each. Extraction is a single non-streaming Messages API call with max_tokens of 64,000. Some calls now run past ten minutes and fail with an SDK error about long non-streaming requests; others return stop_reason: max_tokens with truncated JSON. Line items reference earlier meter ids on other pages. What should you change?

options.text: Lower max_tokens to 16,000 so requests finish inside the ten-minute window, and reject invoices whose output exceeds it.
options.explanation: A 900-line invoice legitimately needs more output than 16,000 tokens, so this converts the intermittent truncation into a guaranteed one for the largest documents and simply drops the customer's biggest invoices. Shortening the allowed output does not make the invoice smaller.

options.text: Switch to streaming, accumulate the deltas, and validate the assembled JSON against the schema once the stream ends.
options.explanation: Streaming is the supported path for long generations: it avoids the SDK's guard against long non-streaming requests, keeps the connection alive as output arrives, and preserves a single request so cross-page meter id references stay in one context. Assembling deltas and validating at the end keeps the schema check where it was.

options.text: Raise the HTTP client timeout to 40 minutes so the non-streaming call can wait for the full output to be generated.
options.explanation: The SDK deliberately refuses non-streaming requests it estimates will exceed ten minutes, so a longer client timeout does not get past the error, and a connection held silent for tens of minutes is prone to being dropped by intermediate proxies. It also leaves the truncation cases unaddressed.

options.text: Split each invoice into one request per page so every call produces a small output that comfortably fits the limits.
options.explanation: Line items refer to meter ids defined on earlier pages, so per-page requests lose the references they need and the extractor either guesses or emits nulls. Reconciling 60 partial outputs and their totals afterwards recreates in your code the consistency the model provides when it sees the document whole.

prompt: Validated extractions are pushed to the procurement ERP through a submit_record tool over an internal API that times out under load. Your retry wrapper resubmits on timeout, and an audit now finds 340 duplicate purchase-order records created over a month, each from a submission that had in fact succeeded before the timeout fired. How should the submission path be made safe to retry?

options.text: Derive an idempotency key from the source document hash and record type and send it with every submit_record call.
options.explanation: A stable key derived from the document lets the ERP recognise a resubmission of the same record and return the original result instead of creating a second one, so retries after a timeout become harmless. This fixes the root cause, ambiguous outcomes on timeout, without giving up the retries that keep the pipeline resilient.

options.text: Retry only when the API returns an explicit 5xx error and treat every timeout as a permanent failure routed to the review queue.
options.explanation: Timeouts under load are the most common transient failure in this pipeline, so refusing to retry them sends a large share of good records to humans for a manual resubmit and lowers throughput. It avoids duplicates by giving up on automation exactly where automation is most needed.

options.text: Before each retry, call a lookup endpoint to check whether a record for that document already exists, and skip the submit if it does.
options.explanation: A check-then-submit sequence has a window in which the original request may still be completing, so the lookup returns nothing and the retry creates a duplicate anyway. It also doubles calls to an API that is already timing out under load, which makes the original problem more frequent.

options.text: Disable automatic retries entirely and have the agent ask a reviewer to confirm each resubmission after a timeout.
options.explanation: The reviewer has no better way than the agent to know whether the first submission landed, so the decision is still a guess, only slower and more expensive. It trades hundreds of automated retries per month for human toil without giving anyone the information that would make the retry safe.

prompt: Your extraction service references the model by its alias rather than a dated snapshot. Three weeks ago the schema-valid rate stayed at 99% but reviewer overturns on the payment_terms field rose from 2% to 9%. The change coincides with the alias moving to a newer snapshot; no prompt or schema was changed. Downstream systems consumed the drifted data for three weeks before anyone noticed. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep using the alias so the service benefits from model improvements automatically, and tune the payment_terms instructions.
options.explanation: Staying on the alias means the next silent move can degrade a different field just as quietly, and tuning instructions against a target that changes underneath you makes the prompt fragile. It treats an uncontrolled dependency change as a prompt problem when the change was the dependency itself.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 for all extraction calls so outputs become deterministic and drift between runs disappears.
options.explanation: Temperature reduces sampling variance within a given model but has no effect on the difference between two model snapshots, which is what changed here. Determinism would make the drifted behaviour more consistent, not more correct, and gives the team no notice when the alias moves again.

options.text: Pin a dated snapshot in production and promote a new one only after it passes the golden set with per-field checks.
options.explanation: Pinning removes the possibility of a silent change, and gating promotion on a golden-set run with per-field metrics turns a model upgrade into a deliberate, tested release like any other dependency bump. The overturn rate on payment_terms would have been caught before production rather than three weeks after.

options.text: Add a dashboard alert on the per-field reviewer overturn rate so a drift of this size is noticed within a day instead of three weeks.
options.explanation: Monitoring shortens the time to detection and is worth having, but it still lets drifted data reach downstream systems before the alarm fires and relies on reviewers sampling the affected field. It reacts to the change after the fact instead of preventing an untested model from taking production traffic.
